title: The guard's hand
hook: Corrie ten Boom, who lost her sister in Ravensbrück, later took the hand of a former guard (The Hiding Place, 1971)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter by two fires, and three questions that answered three denials. Your line was a second chance. Who did you let make it right? Today, the Christian voices step out of scripture and into living memory. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

A church in Munich, after the war. A Dutch woman named Corrie ten Boom has just finished speaking about forgiveness. People are filing out. One man comes forward instead, smiling, with his hand held out, grateful for her message. And she knows his face. In her memoir, The Hiding Place, she tells what came back in that instant: the camp called Ravensbrück, the uniform, the shame of the processing room, and her sister Betsie, who died there. He doesn't seem to remember her. She remembers him. His hand is still out. Today: the guard's hand.
screen: `A CHURCH IN MUNICH.` → `A HAND HELD OUT.` → `SHE KNOWS HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: First, who she was. In The Hiding Place, Corrie tells how her family, Christian watchmakers in the Dutch city of Haarlem, hid Jewish people in their house during the Nazi occupation. They were betrayed and arrested. She and Betsie were sent to Ravensbrück. Betsie, in Corrie's telling, kept talking about forgiveness even in the camp. She did not come home. Second, the moment. In the church, the former guard tells her how grateful he is for her message, that his sins are washed away. Corrie, who has just preached that very message, finds she can't lift her hand. She describes anger and a wish for revenge rising in her, and knowing they were wrong, and being unable to make them go away. That honesty is the heart of the story. The one who taught forgiveness found she couldn't do it on her own. Third, the prayer. In her account, she prays silently, telling Jesus she can't forgive him, and asks for the forgiveness she doesn't have. Then she takes his hand. She describes something like a current running between them, and a love she says was not her own. In her telling, that is the point: forgiveness came as something given to her, not something she produced. Fourth, what it doesn't claim. She doesn't say it was easy, or that the camp didn't matter, or that Betsie's death was somehow fine. She tells it as a struggle she lost before help came. Jesus's own words in Matthew stand behind her: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you." Her story doesn't make that command smaller. It shows how heavy it is, and that one person, at least once, carried it across a church aisle.
screen: `A FAMILY THAT HID NEIGHBORS.` · `SHE COULDN'T LIFT HER HAND.` · `A PRAYER: I CANNOT, GIVE ME YOURS.` · `HARD, NOT SMALL.` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: Take a slower breath than usual, and then another. This one asks for care. Let a very hard forgiveness come to mind, only if you're ready. It might be your own, or someone else's you've watched from close by. You don't have to forgive anything today. Just be honest the way Corrie was: notice what rises when you think of it. Anger, grief, numbness, all of it. Let it be there. Then ask one small question: what would it take, even for a moment, to make this possible? If you pray, you can do what she did and ask for help with what you can't do alone. The bell holds the time.
Ravensbrück. The camp where Corrie ten Boom's sister died, and where the guard whose hand she later took had served. Today's word.
Your line: hard, and possible. Today, when a forgiveness feels impossible, don't force it. Just say the honest thing to yourself: this is hard, and maybe not impossible. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Christians retell Corrie ten Boom's story, from her memoir The Hiding Place, when speaking about forgiving those who did terrible harm.

fork.setup: you're Corrie. a former guard from the camp where your sister died holds out his hand to shake yours. what does she do first?
options: stands frozen, unable to lift her hand.
fork.reveal: she can't lift her hand. only after a silent prayer for help does she take it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saintly woman who forgave easily.
what it means: someone who taught forgiveness found she couldn't do it alone, and asked for help.
what a scholar hears: Corrie's own account doesn't hide the anger; the story's force is the gap between the message she preached and the hand she couldn't lift.

notes: The Hiding Place is under copyright: every detail is paraphrased, nothing quoted. The Munich encounter is also told in her later writings and a magazine article; details vary between versions (e.g. whether he asked directly for forgiveness, which room he guarded). Check against the edition used.
'Love your enemies' is Matthew 5:44 KJV; the KJV verse continues ('do good to them that hate you...'). Quoted portion is exact.
'The shame of the processing room' paraphrases her memory of walking past this man at the camp's processing; confirm against the text.
The index hook names a year (1971) and Ravensbrück; the voice names Ravensbrück (in the book) but gives no year.
Sensitive topic (the Holocaust): told without drama, never as a hook for shock; the practice is explicitly optional. A Keeper should confirm the tone.
